content: Ethyl ether exerts a depressing effect on the central nervous system (CNS) and influences neuromuscular transmission as well as the muscle itself. The mechanism of neuromuscular blocking action of ethyl ether appears to be similar to, but not identical to, that of d-tubocurarine. When both drugs are administered to the same patient, their effects are additive due to synergism. The neuromuscular block induced by ethyl ether is not effectively reversed by edrophonium or succinylcholine, whereas neostigmine has been reported to counteract the effects of ethyl ether on the motor end-plate. The reduction in muscle contractility caused by ethyl ether may be attributed to a pharmacological effect at the level of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. During light ethyl ether anesthesia, salivary and gastric secretions are increased, but they decrease during deep anesthesia. Bowel motility is reduced due to stimulation of dilator fibers and depression of smooth muscle activity. Nausea and vomiting are common after ethyl ether anesthesia, as the agent stimulates the vomiting center in the medulla and irritates the gastric mucosa after being absorbed in saliva and reaching the stomach. The incidence of postoperative nausea varies with the duration of surgery and the depth of anesthesia. Ethyl ether vapor depresses myocardial activity when introduced into the circulation in a heart-lung preparation. Ethyl ether anesthesia increases sympathetic nervous activity in both dogs and humans, with plasma noradrenaline levels rising as the depth of anesthesia increases. It has been suggested that the increase in sympathetic preganglionic activity caused by ethyl ether anesthesia in cats is due to a central action on the medullary vasomotor center or spinal vasomotor neurons. The direct myocardial depressant effect of ethyl ether observed in isolated heart preparations is counteracted by the positive inotropic effects of adrenaline and noradrenaline released during anesthesia. Ethyl ether also appears to inhibit parasympathetic activity in humans. Remarkably, ethyl ether anesthesia produces minimal changes in blood pressure and pulse rate and rarely causes cardiac arrhythmias. In rats, ethyl ether anesthesia initially decreases arterial pressure and total peripheral resistance while increasing the cardiac index. Over time, the cardiac index normalizes, and total peripheral resistance increases. Blood flow to the spleen, stomach, intestines, kidneys, and colon decreases during anesthesia, whereas blood flow to the brain and heart increases. Anesthetic agents, including ethyl ether, can have both direct and hormone-mediated effects on leukocytes. Postoperative leukocytosis has been reported in humans following ethyl ether anesthesia, likely due to its sympathomimetic effects. Blood samples from workers chronically exposed to ethyl ether fumes have shown polycythemia and elevated leukocyte counts in some individuals. Plasma aldosterone levels, plasma renin activity, and plasma antidiuretic hormone levels increase significantly during ethyl ether anesthesia. Ethyl ether anesthesia also causes a significant decrease in serum calcium levels in patients undergoing routine surgical procedures, with levels returning to near normal within 24 hours. The mechanism behind this effect remains unknown. In laboratory animals, ethyl ether anesthesia administered via an ether-saturated jar and maintained with a nose cone for three minutes significantly increases plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) levels. However, this effect is absent in rats with an anterolateral hypothalamic cut and adrenalectomy performed 7–8 days prior, or in rats exposed to ether two hours after an anterolateral cut. These findings suggest that intact neural pathways entering the medial basal hypothalamus from the anterolateral direction are necessary for the ACTH-releasing action of ethyl ether stress. Plasma levels of corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), arginine vasopressin (AVP), oxytocin (OXY), and ACTH double within two minutes of a one-minute exposure to ethyl ether. Plasma CRH levels continue to rise five minutes after exposure, while AVP and OXY return to baseline. Ethyl ether anesthesia does not affect the mean concentrations or dissociation constants of uterine estrogen or progesterone receptors in rats. No differences in plasma thyroxine levels are observed between control rats and those exposed to ethyl ether inhalation for two minutes. Ethyl ether anesthesia increases plasma beta-endorphin-like immunoreactivity, likely of pituitary origin, without significant changes in pituitary or brainstem beta-endorphin content. Treatment of human sera with ethyl ether does not significantly alter immunoglobulin levels, but complement activity is lost. Ethyl ether has been reported to be non-mutagenic in the Salmonella/rat liver microsomal assay system. Additionally, no evidence of genotoxic activity was found for ethyl ether in the Ames reversion test or bacterial DNA-repair test.
